meaning: 'Portion, share' (from aṃśa), one of the twelve Ādityas

phonemes.desc: Short open [ɐ] carrying the anusvāra — a nasal hum closing into the following sibilant.
Voiceless palatal sibilant [ɕ], soft like 'sh' in 'ship', plus a final schwa-like [ɐ].

pronunciation.approximation: UM-shah; the ṃ is a nasal hum, the ś a soft sh.
pronunciation.note: Sanskrit aṃśa carries the anusvāra (ṃ) — a nasalization of the preceding vowel before the sibilant — written with the single dot of the Devanagari अंश. The word means "portion, share," and the restoration Aṃśa keeps the nasal exactly where the phonology and the scripture put it. The anusvāra nasalizes before the sibilant: aṃśa, never amsa — the dot is a sound, not an ornament.

domains.title: The Allotted Share
domains.subtitle: Portion, Sacrifice, and the Twelfth Sun
domains.lead: Aṃśa is the quietest of the twelve Ādityas: the sun as the apportioner, the god whose name simply means "share." In a sacrificial universe where everything — food, merit, cattle, days — is portioned out, Aṃśa is the power that makes the portion just.

cards.name: The Portion
cards.desc: His name is the noun: the share of sacrifice, inheritance, and fate that falls to each.

cards.name: The Twelfth Āditya
cards.desc: One of the twelve solar powers who rule the year's twelve portions.

cards.name: Navāṃśa
cards.desc: His word lives on in astrology: the navāṃśa, the ninth division of every sign.

cards.name: The Sacrifice
cards.desc: The fire ritual where every god receives a measured portion — his office, nightly.

mythology.lead: Aṃśa has no single great narrative — like many Vedic gods, he is a function given face: the apportionment that the sacrifice performs and the year repeats. His mythology is the theology of the share, told by the hymns that divide, the Brāhmaṇas that legislate the division, and the Purāṇas that calendar it.

myths.title: Son of Aditi
myths.text: The Ṛgveda knows the Ādityas as the sons of Aditi — 'the unbound' — the solar powers who guard ṛta, cosmic order, and punish the oath-breaker; hymns such as 2.27 invoke them as the strong sons of the boundless mother, each one a face of the one sun's law. The later tradition counts them as twelve, one for each month of the year, and the roster survives in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (6.6.38–39): Dhātā, Mitra, Aryamā, Śakra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, Bhaga, Vivasvān, Pūṣā, Savitā, Tvaṣṭā, Viṣṇu. Aṃśa stands in the list exactly where his name says he must: among the guardians of the covenant, the enforcers of what is due. A god whose name is the word for 'share' is a theology you can parse at sight — he is the portion, personified, and his inclusion among the law-keeping suns declares that fair division is not bookkeeping but cosmic order.

myths.title: Every God a Share
myths.text: The Vedic sacrifice is an economy of portions. The hymn distributes the offering — 'this share to Agni, this to Soma' — and the Brāhmaṇas legislate that the gods' shares were fixed at the beginning of things: the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.7.3–4) tells how the gods and the anti-gods contended for the sacrifice, how the gods took it for their own and assigned its parts — the ghee, the grains, the portions of the carcass — so that every deity receives the measure that is his. Aṃśa is the personification of that fixing: without the allotted share, no ritual holds, no inheritance stands, no year completes. The deepest grammar of the idea is already in the Puruṣa Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90.11–14), where the gods divide the primal being himself — from whose mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the orders of society arise. Creation, in this vision, is a division; and the share-god is creation's own arithmetic made divine.

myths.title: The Dispute over the Portion
myths.text: The Brāhmaṇas are honest that the gods did not win their shares by innocence alone. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa's telling (1.7.3–4), the gods and the asuras — both children of Prajāpati — strove for the worlds and the sacrifice; the gods prevailed by wit and stratagem, and the asuras were driven down. The myth's lesson is the god's nature: a share is never neutral — it is the shape of justice or of theft, and Aṃśa's name sits on the scale. The same Brāhmaṇic imagination keeps the warning concrete in stories of stolen soma and rigged dice: what is portioned out can be portioned wrongly, and the cosmos notices. This is why the hymns place the share-god among the Ādityas, the guardians of ṛta, rather than among the givers of boons. The share is not a gift but a right; its measure is the oldest form of justice there is — and its theft the oldest crime.

myths.title: The Twelve Suns
myths.text: Purāṇic astronomy assigns each month to one of the twelve Ādityas — the dvādaśāditya of Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.11.27–32, where the sun of each month presides over a season's work from his own station, and the year is the sum of their turns. The Veda had already imaged it: the famous wheel of Ṛgveda 1.164.11, 'set with twelve spokes', upon which seven hundred twenty children of Agni stand — the days and nights riding the year's rim. For Aṃśa the correspondence is exact: the year is the oldest inheritance, and each month its share. His name outlived his cult in the same discipline — Jyotiṣa divides every sign of the zodiac into nine navāṃśa, 'ninth-shares', the harmonic chart without which no horoscope is read. His cult needed no image and no temple: only the accurate turning of the solar year, worshipped every morning in the Gāyatrī that all twelve suns share.

lore.syncretism: He overlaps with Bhaga, the older "dispenser" of shares — the two are so close that Vedic lists sometimes trade their places — and with Mitra and Varuṇa, whose covenant-keeping the Ādityas collectively perform. The comparison that travels farthest is linguistic: Avestan aṃša-, the exact cognate of aṃśa, survives inside the very name Aməša Spənta, the 'Bounteous Immortals' of Zoroastrian theology — the portion raised from common noun to archangel. What in India stayed a quiet solar function became in Iran a rank of cosmic beings; the word crossed the religions intact while the god it named dissolved into his own meaning. Within Hinduism he was never independently worshipped, and needed no adoption: the share-god was already present at every sacrifice, in every portion of ghee measured out by the ladle.
lore.culturalLegacy: His word outlived his cult: aṃśa remains the everyday Sanskrit and Hindi word for "part," and technical vocabularies are built on it — navāṃśa (the ninth harmonic chart in Jyotisha astrology), kalāṃśa in music, daśāṃśa in taxation records. Wherever Indian thought divides a whole into rightful portions — astrology, inheritance law, music theory — the god's name is the operative term. The languages kept what the rituals let go: ask any Hindi speaker how many aṃśa are in a thing, and the share-god answers, unnamed, on every tongue.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Aṃśa is the god of fairness at the smallest scale: not the harvest but the share; not the year but the month; not the whole but the part that is yours. He asks the oldest question of any household, any state, any life: was the portion just — and did you take only your own?

The portion-god is the least dramatic and most daily of the Ādityas, and that is his teaching: justice is mostly arithmetic — the fair share, the counted month, the inheritance divided without sleight. A sacrifice, a will, a budget, a calendar: all are his small liturgies. The hymns place him among the guardians of ṛta, cosmic order, rather than among the givers of boons, because the share is not a gift but a right, and its measure is the oldest form of justice there is. The year turns, the shares are counted, and the sun — the tradition repeats like a refrain — apportions the same light to all. In that daily, unglamorous fairness is the oldest image of justice India has.

lore.archaeology: Early Vedic religion was aniconic: no image of Aṃśa was ever made, and none was wanted — the fire altar was his only temple. The archaeology of the Ādityas is textual and structural: the śrauta fire-altars of the Śulba tradition, laid out with the geometry of portions (the altar's bricks counted and placed by rule), are the material form of his theology. Later Surya temples — Konarak, Modhera — give the solar Ādityas a collective home in stone.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written अंश in Devanagari: the short a, the anusvāra dot above it, then śa. The same spelling covers the god and the common noun "share," which is precisely the theology — the Āditya is the portion, personified.
